opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the thing I keep coming back to is that right now, doing serious work on the internals of neural networks is way harder than it should be. If you're a researcher with a good idea, say a hypothesis about how a model represents some concept, or why it fails on a certain class of inputs, you can easily spend weeks just on infrastructure before you get to the question you actually care about. You're wrangling activations, writing hooks, figuring out how to run things at scale, building visualizations from scratch. Then the next person does it all over again.

So what I want Silico to make possible is for researchers to spend their time on the science, not the plumbing. You should be able to load a model, look at what's happening inside it, form a hypothesis, intervene, and see what changes, in a tight loop. Minutes, not weeks. When that loop gets fast, the kind of research people do changes. You run more experiments, you take more speculative bets, you notice weird things you'd never have stumbled on if each experiment cost you a week.

The bigger hope is that it helps turn interpretability from something closer to artisanal craft into something more like a mature experimental science. Shared tools, reproducible results, people building on each other's findings instead of reimplementing them. If we want to understand these systems well enough to trust them, and to actually steer and improve them, we need far more people doing this work, and far more productively than today. Lowering that barrier is really the whole point.

r001.rationale: The response argues that Silico can speed interpretability research by reducing infrastructure work, but it does not mention coding agents or extend their role in software engineering to scientific research.

r002.rationale: It describes infrastructure and engineering work as slowing research on neural network internals, but does not identify alignment research as the research being impeded.

r003.rationale: The response discusses studying, steering, and improving AI systems, but does not present AI models as tools for building better AI models.

r004.rationale: It hopes to enable more people to do interpretability work, but does not connect that to reducing concentration in who shapes AI’s future.

r005.rationale: It describes a faster cycle of forming hypotheses, intervening, and observing results, but does not propose delegating experiment execution to agents.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short version is: I want a biologist to be able to ask "what happens to this system if I perturb it like so" and get a real answer in minutes instead of months, without first becoming a systems biologist or a computer scientist.

Right now the loop looks like this. You form a hypothesis, you design an experiment, you wait weeks for cells to grow or mice to age, you run the assay, you analyze it, and then you learn whether you were right. The hypothesis-testing step is the expensive part, so people run very few hypotheses. Everyone sort of accepts that you get to test maybe a dozen ideas a year.

Simulation changes the math on that. If you have a model that actually captures the dynamics of the system, you can run a thousand experiments in silico, throw out the nine hundred that are obviously wrong, and spend your wet lab budget on the hundred that are genuinely uncertain. The bench doesn't go away. It becomes the place where you confirm, not the place where you explore.

The thing I keep coming back to is that biology has had the data for a while, but it hasn't had the medium. Physicists had equations. Engineers had CAD. Biologists have had spreadsheets and intuition and a lot of hard-won craft knowledge in people's heads. We want to give them a place where that knowledge becomes an executable object, something you can poke at, share, and have argue back at you when you're wrong.

And honestly, I want it to make the field more honest. When your model is a sentence in a discussion section, nobody can falsify it. When it's a simulation that makes quantitative predictions, you find out fast where your understanding breaks down. That failure is the useful part. Most of what I think Silico will do for researchers is make the failures arrive sooner and cheaper, so the actual discoveries come faster.

r001.rationale: The response proposes simulation to accelerate biological hypothesis testing, but does not extend coding agents’ acceleration of software engineering to scientific research.

r002.rationale: It describes the cost and delay of wet-lab experiments as a bottleneck, but does not identify engineering bottlenecks in alignment research.

r003.rationale: The response discusses biological system simulations, not AI models as tools for building better AI models.

r004.rationale: It aims to make biological modeling more accessible, but does not connect access to building AI models with reducing concentration in shaping AI’s future.

r005.rationale: It proposes running simulated experiments to help prioritize wet-lab work, but does not describe delegating experiment execution to agents so researchers can focus on substantive research questions.

astra-6.text: I want Silico to make it possible for researchers to spend more of their time thinking about the questions that matter to them. You have an idea, you have a hypothesis, and then there’s often this enormous amount of work between that and an experiment that can actually tell you something. I’d like us to make that loop much faster: help you turn the idea into an experiment, understand the result, and figure out what to try next. And ideally, that means a small team can pursue questions that previously would have required resources they just didn’t have.

sol-6.1.text: I want Silico to make it possible for researchers to spend more of their time on the science itself—asking questions, developing hypotheses, and figuring out what the results mean. Ideally, you could take an idea and move quickly into testing it, without getting bogged down in all the work of assembling tools and moving data around. And as that process gets easier, you can explore questions that otherwise might have been too expensive or time-consuming to pursue.
